steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Newspapers are a key media form for informing, influencing, and reflecting public opinion. They combine written, visual, and layout codes to communicate news and comment.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Tabloid vs broadsheet: tabloids (The Sun, Daily Mirror) use sensational stories, large headlines, and simple language for a mass audience. Broadsheets (The Times, Guardian) use in-depth reporting, complex language, and serious analysis for an educated audience.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: News values (Galtung and Ruge): the criteria editors use to select stories — immediacy, proximity, conflict, drama, celebrity, negativity, surprise, and size/threshold.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Newspaper conventions: headline, byline, lead paragraph (who, what, where, when, why), body text, photographs with captions, and page layout (above the fold).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What are Galtung and Ruge's news values? | Q: How do tabloid and broadsheet newspapers differ? | Q: Evaluate the impact of digital technology on newspapers.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: News values are the criteria editors use to decide which stories to publish: immediacy (is it happening now?), proximity (is it local?), conflict (does it involve dispute?), drama (is it dramatic?), c | Tabloids use sensational stories, large headlines, simple language, and focus on celebrity and human interest. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always identify whether a newspaper CSP is tabloid or broadsheet and its political stance Use specific headline examples to analyse language and bias Discuss the regulatory context (IPSO, Leveson) when relevant
